judgments.label: true_positive
judgments.rationale: The element is the image logo_ai_laranja.svg after the paragraph "Converse com" in the NeoFeed AI block below the lead photo. The crop and the screenshot show it is the orange wordmark "NEOFEED AI", so the block reads "Converse com NEOFEED AI". Its alt is "icon search", apparently copied from the search button's icon next to it. I looked for reasons it could pass. The image is not decorative: the product name is only in the image, and the input placeholder "Pergunte para NeoFeed AI" is a separate control. Even if it were decorative, a non-null wrong alt fails under F39. The image is not inside a link or button that names it. The live HTML fetched today has the same img with alt="icon search", so the capture matches. The alternative gives a screen-reader user "Converse com icon search" instead of the product name, which fails 1.1.1 (F30, an alternative that is not an alternative). Read in good faith, the claim that the alt does not give what the image conveys names this failure.

judgments.label: true_positive
judgments.rationale: The element is the newsletter sign-up field <input type="email" name="EMAIL" placeholder="Seu melhor e-mail"> under "Receba o NeoFeed no seu e-mail" (Mailchimp for WP form). It asks for the user's own email address, which is the 'email' purpose in WCAG's Input Purposes list. It has no autocomplete attribute: none in the snapshot's rendered DOM, and none in the live HTML fetched today, where no script adds one. I checked possible ways it could pass. type="email" sets only the data format, not that the address is the user's own, and Understanding 1.3.5 names autocomplete (H98) as the way to meet the criterion in HTML. A form-level autocomplete cannot carry a purpose token, and the form has none anyway. The snapshot records Chromium's issue FormInputAssignedAutocompleteValueToIdOrNameAttributeError on the field, so the claim's last sentence is also true. The field fails 1.3.5 for the reason the claim gives.

judgments.label: false_positive
judgments.rationale: The element is the last icon in the share row under the byline (desktop copy). The image mail.svg, alt "mail icone", is all a link holds whose href, after Cloudflare's email decoding, is mailto:?subject=<article title>&body=<article URL>. The link opens the user's mail program to send the article. With the image replaced by its alternative (the G82 and R2 test), the link reads "mail icone", which names where it goes: email. The extra word "icone" is noise, but it does not hide the purpose. The sibling links "whatsapp icone", "linkedin icone", "Facebook icone" and "X icone" follow the same pattern, and Rampa did not flag them. An alt like "Compartilhar por e-mail" would be better practice, but 1.1.1 asks only for a name that describes the control's purpose, and "mail" does that for a mailto link. The live HTML has the same img and alt. In the screenshot a floating video ad covers this icon, but that does not affect the alternative. The claim that the alt does not say where the link leads is wrong, and the model had the href and the sibling links to see it.

judgments.label: true_positive
judgments.rationale: This is the second copy of the NeoFeed AI block, after the TAGS line at the end of the article. The image logo_ai_laranja.svg shows the wordmark "NEOFEED AI" (crop and screenshot) after "Converse com", and its alt is "icon search". It is the same defect as the block at the top. The product name is only in the image. The image is not decorative, and a wrong non-null alt would fail even if it were (F39). No link, button or label around it supplies the name. The live HTML has the same markup, so the capture matches what users receive. The alternative does not present what the image conveys, so the image fails 1.1.1, and the claim names that failure in good faith.
